title: CrazyFlie Trajectory Planning and Control in a Maze
subtitle: Quadrotor controller, waypoint planner, and trajectory generation on real hardware
summary: Deployed a full CrazyFlie 2.0 stack for stable hover, gain tuning, waypoint planning, and maze navigation with VICON tracking feedback.

glance.oneLiner: End-to-end CrazyFlie 2.0 stack with tuned control, A* + RDP waypoint planning, and piecewise-linear trajectory execution in a maze.
glance.problem: Deliver reliable maze navigation on real hardware by updating gains, planning collision-free paths from a voxel map, and keeping flight stable under VICON feedback and hardware limits.
glance.approach: Tuned geometric PD gains on hardware, then generated A* waypoint paths on a 3D occupancy grid, simplified them with RDP, and executed piecewise-linear segments with speed caps and obstacle inflation.
glance.results: Stable hover and waypoint tracking were achieved, and full maze runs were executed; tracking errors appeared at sharp turns due to thrust limits, VICON occlusions, and mass-model mismatch.
takeaways: Real-world tuning and mass-accurate gains are critical for reliable tracking.
RDP + piecewise-linear planning is fast but produces $C^0$ trajectories that stress the motors on sharp turns.
Safety margins and map resolution help avoid collisions but trade off speed and smoothness.
VICON dropouts can dominate tracking error near obstacles.

sections.title: System Overview
paragraphs: This project deploys a full CrazyFlie 2.0 stack on real hardware, spanning a controller, waypoint planner, and trajectory generator, with VICON tracking providing pose feedback and onboard IMU data streamed to the ground station.

Building on earlier coursework in control and planning, we tuned gains for stable hover and aggressive maneuvers, then executed maze navigation by replanning paths and tightening safety margins to balance speed, smoothness, and collision avoidance.

sections.title: Methods
paragraphs: We use a geometric nonlinear controller that aligns the body $z$-axis with the desired thrust direction. The PD position law is $$\ddot{r}^{des} = \ddot{r}_T - K_d(\dot{r}-\dot{r}_T) - K_p(r-r_T).$$

Desired acceleration and thrust satisfy $$m\ddot{r}^{des} + \begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\mg\end{bmatrix} = u_1 R \begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\1\end{bmatrix},$$ so we define $$F^{des} = m\ddot{r}^{des} + \begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\1\end{bmatrix}, \quad u_1 = R\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\1\end{bmatrix}F^{des}.$$

Orientation is set by aligning thrust with the desired body axis and yaw with the target heading: $$c_3^{des} = \frac{F^{des}}{\lVert F^{des} \rVert}, \quad a_\psi = \begin{bmatrix}\cos\psi_T\\\sin\psi_T\\0\end{bmatrix},$$ $$c_2^{des} = \frac{c_3^{des}\times a_\psi}{\lVert c_3^{des}\times a_\psi \rVert}, \quad R^{des} = \begin{bmatrix}c_2^{des} \times c_3^{des} & c_2^{des} & c_3^{des}\end{bmatrix}.$$

The attitude error and angular velocity error are $$e_R = \frac{1}{2}(R^{des^T}R - R^T R^{des})^\vee, \quad e_\omega = \omega - \omega^{des},$$ and the moment command is $$u_2 = I(-K_R e_R - K_\omega e_\omega).$$

We tuned four gains in simulation and then finalized them on hardware. The values below are the diagonals of 3x3 gain matrices, with gains scaled down about 30% from simulation to account for mass and actuation differences.

afterParagraphs: The y-direction step test indicates a settling time around 2 s, a rise time around 1.1 s, steady-state error near 2%, and a damping ratio near 0.4. The response is underdamped and initially slow to settle, and we also observed a z-axis mismatch that was corrected with additional hardware tuning.

sections.title: Trajectory Generation
paragraphs: We discretize the workspace into a voxel occupancy grid and plan a waypoint path with A* over the 3D graph. Edge cost is Euclidean distance and the heuristic is the $\ell_2$ distance to the goal: $$c(\text{current}, \text{neighbor}) = \bigl\lVert \text{neighbor} - \text{current} \bigr\rVert, \quad h(n) = \bigl\lVert n - \text{goal} \bigr\rVert, \quad f(n) = g(n) + h(n).$$ The search expands the lowest-cost node, relaxes neighbors, and backtracks parent pointers to recover a discrete path in $(x,y,z)$.

We simplify the path with Ramer-Douglas-Peucker using $\varepsilon = 0.1\,\text{m}$, then generate a piecewise linear trajectory between waypoints: $$\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{p}_i + \mathbf{v}_i (t - t_{\mathrm{start}, i}), \quad \mathbf{v}_i = v_i\,\frac{\mathbf{p}_{i+1} - \mathbf{p}_i}{\lVert \mathbf{p}_{i+1} - \mathbf{p}_i \rVert}, \quad T_i = \frac{\lVert \mathbf{p}_{i+1} - \mathbf{p}_i \rVert}{v_i}.$$

Because each segment uses constant velocity, the trajectory is $C^0$-continuous and exhibits velocity jumps at segment boundaries. We mitigate this by capping speed below 1 m/s and adjusting $v_i$ based on segment length and turn angle. With a 0.2 m obstacle inflation margin and $\Delta x = \Delta y = \Delta z = 0.25\,\text{m}$ resolution, the resulting waypoints remain safely away from obstacles while keeping computation fast.

sections.title: Maze Flight Experiments
paragraphs: We ran three maze flights and compared planned paths against logged trajectories. Figure IV shows Maps 1-3 (left to right) with world obstacles, planned trajectories, waypoints, and actual flight paths.

Across all three maps we observe deviations between the planned trajectory and the flown path, especially near sharp turns and obstacle-adjacent maneuvers. The main drivers are limited thrust (curvature tracking limits), VICON occlusions that cause brief state-estimation dropouts, and small mass mismatches that degrade PID tuning during faster segments.

To improve reliability and speed, we would retune gains using real mass and logs, adopt higher-order spline trajectories to smooth velocity and acceleration, and increase map resolution for more precise path optimization. With more time, adaptive gain scheduling based on tracking error could further stabilize flight through the maze while preserving speed.

sections.title: Takeaways
paragraphs: This project shows that a full CrazyFlie planning and control stack can succeed on real hardware when perception, planning, and control are tuned together. The dominant errors came from hardware limits and state-estimation dropouts rather than the planner, reinforcing the need for gain tuning with real mass/logs, safety margins aligned with motor limits and estimation jitter, and smoother trajectories to avoid sudden thrust demands.
